account: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York randomized colorectal and gynecology operations scheduled between 7 April and 25 June 2018 on two surgical campuses. For half of the cases, schedulers used case durations predicted by an in-house machine learning model the day before surgery; the other half used the usual EHR estimate adjusted by surgeons or schedulers. Among 683 patients, the mean absolute error of the planned duration fell from 59.3 minutes to 49.5 minutes. The start delay for following cases, which is the time patients waited in the presurgical area, fell by 33.1 minutes per patient, from 49.4 to 16.3 minutes. Time between cases did not change. The model was built and tested by the hospital's own staff at a single cancer center, and the trial covered two surgical services.

ai_role.statement: Cases were randomized to model-based or usual duration estimates, stratified by surgeon and operating room location, so the comparison isolates the model's estimates.

claim_basis: Sources: one independent peer-reviewed study and the makers' peer-reviewed study. The cited evidence includes no finding by a regulator or court.

comparator.quote: Of the 683 patients included, those assigned to the machine learning algorithm had significantly lower mean (SD) absolute error (control group, 59.3 [72] minutes; intervention group, 49.5 [66] minutes; difference, -9.8 minutes; P = .03) compared with the control group.
